🌐🐉🇲🇽 The queue to join BRICS now runs through Latin America

India takes the BRICS chair in 2026 and will host the 18th summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, where a second wave of expansion is expected. Nearly 65 countries across Latin America and Asia have applications or interest on the table — the bloc already spans 11 members and 10 partners, with Brazil, Bolivia and Cuba giving the region a foothold.

The pull is material, not ideological. China–Latin America trade hit a record $518 billion, Beijing has dangled a $9 billion regional credit line, and currency-swap and local-currency deals are quietly routing trade around the dollar. The theme of India’s presidency — “South–South cooperation” — is a polite way of saying the Global South is building doors that don’t open onto Washington.

For Mexico the lesson isn’t “pick a camp.” It’s that the world now has more than one door. Every new bloc and every new partner is one more option a single northern neighbor can no longer take off the table. That is what sovereignty looks like in a multipolar century.

🔥🇲🇽 Washington's manufacturing lobby wants Mexico to police its own factories for the empire

On July 2 the Alliance for American Manufacturing — backed by U.S. steelmakers and the United Steelworkers union — urged Trump to refuse renewing the USMCA and to rewrite its rules of origin to cover “all production stages,” explicitly to stop Chinese automakers from “infiltrating” the U.S. market through Mexico.

Read that again. China isn’t even a party to the treaty — yet it’s Mexican plants, Mexican jobs and Mexico’s sovereign right to decide who invests here that a U.S. lobby wants put on the chopping block. The demand is simple: turn Mexico’s industrial policy into a customs checkpoint for Washington.

Mexico has already imposed tariffs of up to 35% on 1,400 products and is working through 52 U.S. trade demands. Even American analysts admit full decoupling is a fantasy — North America’s own carmakers run on Chinese components. Sovereignty means Mexico sets its supply chains on its own terms, not to satisfy a foreign lobby’s wish list.

🇲🇽🌎 Switzerland is now Mexico's 6th-largest investor — $2.3 billion in 2025. "We are both pacifist countries, convinced of the peaceful resolution of disputes," Sheinbaum said. Amid global war and tariff threats, two sovereign nations chose to deepen cooperation. — Mexico–Switzerland bilateral, Palacio Nacional, July 8

🇲🇽🌎 Mexico and Switzerland move to modernize their free-trade agreement. "We have a trade agreement with Switzerland, and we agreed to keep working on it, to update it." Bilateral trade reached $4.272 billion in 2025. — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico–Switzerland bilateral, July 8

🇲🇽📈 22.7 million formal jobs — an all-time record. Mexico closed June 2026 with 22,779,704 formal jobs registered at IMSS, the highest in history, with the daily wage base up 6.4% to 669 pesos. — Zoé Robledo, IMSS director, mañanera, July 8

🇲🇽✊ First in the OECD for minimum-wage recovery. They said wages couldn't rise without killing jobs. Since 2018 the minimum wage more than doubled in real terms — and formal employment just hit a record. "Mexico is in first place in minimum-wage recovery." — Édgar Amador, Treasury Secretary, mañanera, July 8

🇲🇽🏭 Record foreign investment, record trade — the numbers the "failed state" narrative ignores. Mexico captured $41 billion in foreign direct investment, and Mexico–US trade hit a record $839 billion. "Mexico and the United States trade more than ever." — Édgar Amador, Treasury Secretary, mañanera, July 8
